bib.title: Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?", Jia He, Mukund Rungta, David Koleczek, Arshdeep Sekhon, Franklin X Wang, Sadid Hasan (Microsoft, MIT). arXiv:2411.10541v1, 15 Nov 2024. Preprint, short paper (16 pages).

COVERAGE: 46,926 of 46,926 chars read (all pages: body, limitations, related work, appendices A-E with Tables 3-8, references skimmed). Extraction is clean for text and tables. I did not fetch the figure images. Figure content is described only from captions and text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Format alone changes accuracy a lot on GPT-3.5-turbo, and the best format differs by task. GPT-3.5 does best with JSON on MMLU and HumanEval, and worst with Markdown on MMLU.
  number: MMLU 59.7 (JSON) vs 50.0 (Markdown), p<0.001; HumanEval 59.8 (JSON) vs 40.2 (Plain text).
  setup: gpt-35-turbo-0613, one-sided matched-pair t-test of best vs worst format. MMLU test set is 14,079 questions, accuracy. HumanEval is all 164 problems, pass@1. Content is held fixed across formats.
  quote: "MMLU 59.7(JSON) 50.0(Markdown) < 0.001 59.4(JSON) 50.7(Markdown) < 0.001" and "HumanEval 59.8(JSON) 40.2(Plain text) < 0.001 57.9(JSON) 37.20(Plain text) < 0.001"
  where: Table 1, p.3; Tables 3-4, p.13
- Claim: GPT-4 is much less sensitive to format than GPT-3.5, as measured by the coefficient of mean deviation (CMD) across the four formats.
  number: GPT-4-1106-preview CMD below 0.036 on all benchmarks; GPT-4-32k-0613 not above 0.043; GPT-3.5 series 0.035 to 0.176.
  setup: CMD = sum|s(pi)-mean|/(n*mean) over 4 formats, 6 benchmarks, 4 Azure GPT models. Read from Figure 6.
  quote: "the GPT-4-1106-preview model exhibits superior robustness to format changes, maintaining a performance dispersion consistently below 0.036 across all benchmarks." "The GPT-3.5 series displays a broader range of CMDs, from 0.035 to 0.176"
  where: App. D.2, p.12
- Claim: Outputs under different formats often disagree. GPT-3.5 gives identical answers across formats rarely; GPT-4 is more consistent.
  number: GPT-3.5 consistency scores below 0.5; 16% identical responses between Markdown and JSON; GPT-4 scores above 0.5.
  setup: MMLU, temperature 0, consistency = fraction of test items with identical answers for two templates. FIND is in Fig 8.
  quote: "The GPT-3.5-turbo series displayed low consistency, with scores below 0.5, and only 16% identical responses between Markdown and JSON formats. In contrast, GPT-4's consistency scores surpassed 0.5"
  where: Sec 4.2, p.3
- Claim: No single format is best across models. GPT-3.5 prefers JSON and GPT-4 prefers Markdown. Format preferences transfer poorly across model versions and well within one sub-series.
  number: IoU of top-template sets often below 0.2 across series; above 0.7 within the same sub-series.
  setup: IoU over sets of statistically indistinguishable top templates (matched-pair t-test). Figure 3 is NER Finance.
  quote: "we found low compatibility between different model series, with IoU often below 0.2. However, models from the same sub-series, like GPT-35-turbo-16k-0613 and GPT-35-turbo-0613, show high IoU over 0.7."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.3-4
- Claim: A worst-case format collapse. GPT-4-32k-0613 on HumanEval with JSON drops far below the other formats because it writes its chain of thought and then does not write the code.
  number: 21.95 (JSON) vs 76.22 (Plain text); Markdown 75.61, YAML 68.29.
  setup: gpt-4-32k-0613, HumanEval, 164 problems, pass@1. The authors read the outputs; the other models did not do this. The "laziness" explanation is a hypothesis.
  quote: "76.2(Plain text) 21.95(JSON) < 0.001" and "the model would generate chain of thought in plain text, but did not continue with actually generating the code."
  where: Table 1 p.3; Table 4 and App. D.2 p.12-13
- Claim: In the authors' text, headline swings are 200% on FIND and over 300% on HumanEval.
  number: 200%, over 300%.
  setup: FIND is GPT-3.5 moving from Markdown to plain text (about 5.2 to 15.9, roughly 3x). HumanEval is gpt-4-32k moving from JSON to plain text.
  quote: "a dramatic 200% improvement when prompts are switched from Markdown to plain text" and "a performance boost of over 300% when the prompt format is changed from JSON to plain text"
  where: Sec 3.2, p.3
  Caveat: from Table 4, 76.22/21.95 is 3.47x, a +247% gain, not "over 300%". Check before citing.
- Claim: Sensitivity is statistically significant almost everywhere.
  number: All p-values below 0.05 except GPT-4-1106-preview on HumanEval (p=0.055).
  setup: 4 models x 7 benchmark tasks (the 6 benchmarks, with CODEXGLUE split into two directions). GPT-4-1106 on HumanEval spans 82.9 to 86.6.
  quote: "All p-values are below 0.05, except for GPT-4-1104-preview on HumanEval, confirming widespread prompt format sensitivity."
  where: Table 1 caption, p.3
- Claim: The sensitivity is general. It appears in all four MMLU domains, so it does not depend on the skill the task needs.
  number: none
  setup: MMLU per-domain breakdown (humanities, social science, STEM, other), Figure 5.
  quote: "the model's sensitivity to prompt formatting is a general characteristic, rather than being contingent on the specific skills or reasoning abilities required by different tasks."
  where: App. D.1, p.9-10
- Claim: Format ranking is task-dependent. Examples: NER Finance favors plain text for GPT-3.5 and YAML for GPT-4. Code translation favors structured formats and penalizes plain text.
  number: NER Finance GPT-3.5-0613 37.20 plain vs 24.60 YAML; GPT-4-1106 53.8 YAML vs 49.3 plain. CODEXGLUE Java2CS GPT-3.5 78.4 JSON vs 66.5 plain. HumanEval-X 69.8 YAML vs 63.0 plain.
  setup: Same models; NER Finance is 500 sampled items; CODEXGLUE is 1000 items scored by BLEU; HumanEval-X is Java to Python, BLEU.
  quote: "NER Finance 37.2(Plain text) 24.6(Y AML) < 0.001" and "CODEXGLUE (Java2CS) 78.4 (JSON) 66.5 (Plain text)"
  where: Table 1 p.3; Tables 5, 7, 8 p.13
- Claim: In the intro's Figure 1 example, one JSON vs Markdown change moves accuracy by 42%.
  number: 42%
  setup: gpt-35-turbo-16k-0613, MMLU international-law multiple-choice subset. This is not in the tables; the 42% is probably relative.
  quote: "Accuracy goes up by 42% for JSON compared to Markdown."
  where: Fig 1 caption, p.1
- Claim (abstract headline): up to 40% variation for GPT-3.5-turbo on code translation.
  number: 40%
  quote: "GPT-3.5-turbo's performance varies by up to 40% in a code translation task depending on the prompt template"
  where: Abstract
  Caveat: I could not reproduce 40% from Tables 7-8. The largest code-translation gap I can compute for GPT-3.5 is 66.46 to 78.37 BLEU (about 18% relative, 12 points). The 40% may refer to HumanEval (40.24 to 59.76 is +48% relative), which is generation, not translation. Treat as unverified.

PROMPT DESIGN (for prompt anatomy)
Every prompt has five components: persona, task instructions, examples, output format instructions, user ask. Contents are identical across formats. Only structure and syntax differ.
  quote: "Prompts include five components: persona, task instructions, examples, output format instructions, and user ask."
  where: Sec 2.2, p.2. Templates in Table 2 (p.9) and App. C (p.9-11).
Two kinds of change are bundled in the formats. The plain-text system prompt is one paragraph. Markdown, YAML and JSON also split the content into labeled sections. The authors do not separate the two effects.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: only OpenAI GPT models (via Azure); no LLaMA, Gemini, PaLM or Phi. HTML and XML were not tried. Everything else was held constant, including few-shot count and instruction precision. They suggest interaction with those factors as future work.
- Not shown: no explanation of why. Their ideas about "last hidden layer" robustness and the GPT-4-turbo laziness fix are speculation.
- No seeds, variance or prompt-wording variants are reported beyond the paired t-tests. The ± values in Tables 3-8 appear to be standard errors or deviations, not defined.
- Dated: models are 2023 snapshots (gpt-35-turbo-0613, gpt-4-0613, gpt-4-1106-preview). Modern models are likely less sensitive, but the paper does not show it. As of 2026-11 these are all superseded.
- Internal inconsistencies, so check numbers before citing:
  - Table 1 GPT-4-1106 Cs2Java lists 83.1 (JSON), but Table 8 shows 75.00. The 83.05 value is in the GPT-4-32k column.
  - Table 1 GPT-4-1106 Java2CS lists 77.0 (Markdown); Table 8 shows 74.16.
  - Table 1 HumanEval-X lists 72.4 (JSON); Table 7 shows 72.30.
  - Table 1 FIND for GPT-4-1106 has p<0.0269, typed as a p-value.
  - Table 1 and Table 3 agree on the MMLU numbers.
- The "40%", "200%" and "300%" claims are loose relative changes that do not match the tables exactly (see above).

BUILDS ON: Sclar et al., 2023 (spurious features in prompt design, "How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting"); Voronov et al., 2024 (Mind your format); Shu et al., 2023 (consistency metric, psychometric reliability); Aghajanyan, June 2023 tweet (MMLU jump of 6-10 points from "(a)" formatting); Sui et al., 2024 (Table meets LLM, tabular formats, the closest prior work); Liu et al., 2023 (Lost in the middle) and Lu et al., 2022 / Zhao et al., 2021 (ordering of examples and context). Datasets: Hendrycks et al., 2020 (MMLU); Chen et al., 2021 (HumanEval); Schwettmann et al., 2023 (FIND); Lu et al., 2021 (CODEXGLUE); Zheng et al., 2023 (HumanEval-X); OpenAI Evals 2023 (NER Finance).

CODE: none. Table 2 (p.9) has the four template skeletons. The Markdown template is "## Persona / ## Instructions / ## Examples / ## Output Format / ## User Question". The JSON template has keys "Persona", "Instructions", "Examples", "Output format" and a separate object {"User ask"}. App. C (p.9-11) has full NER Finance prompts in all four formats.

FIGURES (captions from text; images not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p.1): same MMLU international-law question in Markdown vs JSON, with accuracy up 42% for JSON on gpt-35-turbo-16k. It is the fastest illustration of the effect.
- Fig 2 (p.4) and Fig 8 (p.15): consistency heatmaps across format pairs for MMLU and FIND. GPT-3.5 is below 0.5, GPT-4 above.
- Fig 3 (p.4) and Fig 7 (p.14): IoU of top templates across models, NER Finance and others.
- Fig 4 (p.11) and Fig 9 (p.16): dotplots of per-format performance on every benchmark. Fig 9 covers all of them. Best for showing format ranking changing by model.
- Fig 5 (p.11): MMLU performance spread per domain.
- Fig 6 (p.12): CMD per model per dataset. It shows the GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 robustness gap.
Tables 3-8 (p.13) hold the raw numbers and are probably more useful than the figures.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Table 1 extraction is slightly garbled for CODEXGLUE rows (values split across lines), but I read it. Figures were not rendered. The tool-result file was truncated once in the first call and I read it in full from a saved file plus a second range 30000-46926. Nothing was skipped.
